narrative_md:
**The April 2024 triple-lock uprating added roughly £11 billion to annual state pension spending — more than the entire Home Office grant to the Metropolitan Police, in a single policy decision.**

The triple-lock — pensions rise by the highest of CPI, average earnings or 2.5% — was a 2010 coalition pledge that has survived every subsequent manifesto. The April 2024 uprating of 8.5% cost an extra £11 billion. State pension spending is on track to exceed £160bn in 2025-26, over 30% of total welfare. The demographic arithmetic says the policy cannot hold another decade. The political arithmetic says every party has pledged otherwise.

**Origins.** The triple-lock was introduced by the 2010 Coalition. Basic State Pension would rise each April by the highest of: (a) inflation (CPI), (b) average earnings, or (c) 2.5%. The logic was pension-catch-up: UK state pensions had eroded relative to earnings through the 1980s-2000s under earnings-link breaks and RPI-vs-CPI switches. The new State Pension (for post-2016 retirees) inherited the same lock from 2016.

**The suspension.** In 2022 the earnings leg was suspended for one year — the COVID job-retention scheme had distorted earnings statistics (furloughed workers returning to full pay created an 8%+ earnings print) and the Sunak-Truss Treasury used a 'double lock' for April 2022 (CPI or 2.5%, not earnings). The earnings leg returned in April 2023.

**The April 2024 uprating.** The September 2023 earnings growth figure of 8.5% was higher than CPI of 6.7%. The triple-lock delivered 8.5%. Basic State Pension rose from £156.20/week to £169.50/week; new State Pension from £203.85/week to £221.20/week. Annual cost: around £11bn in-year increase to state pension spend. Cumulative cost of the triple-lock vs CPI-only since 2010: the IFS estimates £11-12bn per year above what earnings-linkage or CPI-only would have delivered.

**The demography.** UK pensionable-age population (currently 12.8m for State Pension age 66, rising to age 67 from 2026-28) is projected by ONS to reach 15.4m by 2046. Working-age-to-pensioner ratio was 3.5:1 in 2010; is 3.1:1 in 2024; projected 2.7:1 by 2045. State pension spending, at 5.0% of GDP in 2024-25, is projected by the OBR to reach 7.3% of GDP by 2060 on current policy — a 2.3-percentage-point GDP rise, roughly equivalent to another department the size of Defence.

**The 2024 manifestos.** Conservatives pledged 'Triple Lock Plus' — guaranteeing the Personal Allowance would also rise with pensions to keep state pension below the income-tax threshold (a policy response to Treasury's Personal Allowance freeze pulling pensioners into basic-rate). Labour pledged the triple-lock for the full Parliament. Lib Dems, Greens, Reform all pledged preservation. No mainstream party proposed reform.

**The October 2024 and March 2025 Budgets.** Reeves confirmed the triple-lock and applied a 4.1% uprating from April 2025. The Personal Allowance freeze to 2027-28 was not extended — Treasury's fiscal logic recognising the interaction. But no structural reform was announced.

**What the mainstream reform options look like.** (1) Earnings-link: drop CPI and 2.5% legs, retain earnings alone — IFS estimate saves around £6bn/year by 2030. (2) Means-test above certain income: politically toxic, small saving. (3) Raise State Pension age faster (the 2023 Cridland Review recommended 68 between 2037-39; accelerated to 2032-34 would save £8-10bn/year). (4) Smoothed earnings lock (moving average): technical but politically feasible. The Pensions Commission under Baroness Drake, revived in 2025 with Nick Timmins and others, is expected to report 2026. Its mandate quietly includes reviewing the triple-lock for the first time since 2010.
